dataset.name: echo_ground_truth_v1
description: 40 notes as they would actually exist in a working creative's second brain; half-finished article drafts, voice memos with filler words and trailing thoughts, image-sourced quotes, mood board captions, unconnected observations about daily life, and fragments that go nowhere. Semantic relationships span all three tiers, including genuine NONE pairs where no connection exists.
Notes and annotation justifications generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 2026-06-01
Prompt used to generate notes and annotations:

' Can you fill in this dataset of notes for the testing phase of my project? I am testing semantical embedding models with the precision@5 metric for an app that will be able to find connections between notes and link them. Notes will come in multiple formats such as audio and image but will be pre-processed by WhisperAI, Blip and SuryaOCR.The topic should be on creative writing. Imagine a dataset sparsed with half thought-out articles, image snippets for inspiration, random quotes in text/audio/image form, random unconnected thoughts about any topic in text-image/audio form etc.'

annotation_schema.STRONG: The core subject is the same or directly builds on the same idea. A user would almost certainly want to navigate from one note to the other.
annotation_schema.WEAK: The notes share a theme or domain but address different aspects of it. The connection is plausible but not the first thing a user would look for.
annotation_schema.NONE: No meaningful connection. A user navigating from one note would not expect to arrive at the other.

note_types_used.text: Raw typed note: body is the direct content
note_types_used.audio: Voice memo: body is the Whisper transcript, embedding_text includes transcript
note_types_used.image: Embedded image: body is user annotation (may be null), embedding_text is concatenation of BLIP caption + Surya OCR text + body

clusters.C5: Quoted material: typed, photographed, or recorded
clusters.C7: Unconnected daily life observations and thoughts
clusters.C8: Mood board images and visual inspiration

notes.title: In medias res — why it works
notes.body: Starting in the middle forces the reader to do work. They arrive into a situation already in motion and the gap between what they know and what they need to know creates forward pull. The backstory only matters once we care about the character it belongs to. Maybe the better principle is: never explain what you can dramatise, never dramatise what the reader will infer.

notes.title: Non-linear time — draft fragment
notes.body:
There is a difference between a story told out of order and a story that uses time as a material. Shuffling chronology for shock or mystery is a trick. Using time as a thematic substance — where the structure of the narrative enacts what the story is about — is something else. If a character cannot escape their past, the story might need to be told backwards. The form should be the argument.

notes.title: Endings — what they actually need to do
notes.body: An ending doesn't need to resolve everything. It needs to feel inevitable in retrospect while being surprising in the moment. Those two things sound contradictory but aren't. The surprise is in the specific way the inevitability arrives — not whether it arrives. A bad ending explains. A good ending completes.

notes.title: Characters who lie to themselves
notes.body: The most interesting characters are not the ones who lie to the reader — they are the ones who lie to themselves in ways the reader can see through. The gap between what the character believes about themselves and what the narrative reveals is where the dramatic irony lives. The reader knows something the character doesn't know about the character. That knowledge creates a kind of anxious tenderness.

notes.title: First person unreliable — draft notes for essay
notes.body:
What makes a narrator unreliable is not that they lie. Anyone can lie. What makes them unreliable in the interesting literary sense is that the reader can access a layer of truth the narrator cannot. The narrator's blind spots are structural, not strategic. Stevens in Remains of the Day doesn't deceive us — he deceives himself, and the prose style is the evidence. The gap between what he says and what he means is the entire novel.

notes.title: How people talk when nervous
notes.body: Nervous people repeat themselves in slightly different words. They agree with their own sentences. They ask questions they already know the answer to. They are the last person to notice that they've changed the subject. Dialogue that captures this doesn't look like realistic speech — it looks slightly stylised in a specific direction. The texture of self-interruption without the noise of it.

notes.title: Sentence rhythm — something I keep ignoring
notes.body: Long sentences accumulate weight; they carry the reader forward on momentum and the ending lands harder because the journey to it was longer. Short sentences stop. They force breath. They create silence on the page. The paragraph itself can have a rhythm — three long, one short, two long — and the reader feels it even when they can't name it. I need to read my drafts out loud more.

notes.title: The problem with adjectives
notes.body: Adjectives are a way of telling the reader what to think before they've had the chance to think it. The 'dark forest' instructs. The forest that swallows the light behind you at a certain hour — that creates. The instruction forecloses imagination; the image opens it. The test: could the noun stand alone and do more work? If yes, remove the adjective and trust the reader.

notes.title: On metaphor — rough
notes.body:
A metaphor that calls attention to itself has failed. The reader should feel the comparison land before they see the mechanism. Like a stage magician — the trick works only while you're watching the wrong hand. A metaphor that makes you think 'what a good metaphor' is a metaphor that broke the spell.

notes.title: Writer's block is a symptom
notes.body: I don't think writer's block exists as its own condition. What gets called writer's block is usually one of three things: not knowing what happens next (a structural problem), caring too much about writing well to write badly (a perfectionism problem), or not wanting to confront what the next scene requires emotionally (an avoidance problem). The solution to each is completely different. Calling all three by the same name delays the diagnosis.

notes.title: Morning pages — does it actually work?
notes.body:
Been doing morning pages for three weeks. Initial observation: the first page is always garbage and that's the point — it drains the anxious preamble that otherwise appears in the first paragraph of everything I write. By the third page something occasionally surfaces that I didn't know I thought. The value isn't the pages themselves. It's that writing badly on purpose for twenty minutes makes writing carefully afterwards feel like relief rather than pressure.

[[ update after 3 months: yes. keep doing it. ]]

notes.title: Random: deadlines are load-bearing
notes.body: Every piece I've finished, I've finished because something external forced the decision that it was done. Left to my own devices I would revise indefinitely, which means never publish. The deadline doesn't just create urgency — it gives me permission to stop. The external constraint is doing something I apparently can't do for myself: declaring the thing complete.

notes.title: Le Guin — on the reader
notes.body:
"The reader, reading it, makes it live: a live thing, a story." — Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft

The writer provides a score. The reader performs it. No two performances are the same. This is why 'what the author intended' is an interesting question but not a limiting one.

notes.title: Baldwin — on the purpose of art
notes.body:
"Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced." — James Baldwin

Saved this initially for an essay about social fiction but I keep returning to it as a statement about what writing is for at all. Art as a technology for facing things. The story creates the conditions for the confrontation the reader couldn't otherwise access.

notes.title: Essay draft — why genre fiction matters, opening
notes.body:
There is a tendency in discussions of literary fiction to treat genre as a container for lesser ambitions — as though the thriller, the fantasy, the romance are categories of diminished expectation rather than frameworks for different kinds of truth. This is wrong, and the wrongness is worth examining carefully, because it reveals something about the class anxieties that travel with the word 'literary' in a way that the word 'story' does not.

notes.title: Draft — reading as resistance, first para only
notes.body:
We live inside a system that profits from the conversion of attention into data. The book — specifically the physical book, unconnected, untracked, unable to know whether you finished it or skipped to the end — is one of the few remaining technologies that cannot be optimised against you. Reading it is not a retreat. It is a refusal.

notes.title: Voice memo — describing a painting for the collection
notes.generated_transcript: I'm in the gallery and I can't take photos so I'm just going to describe this. it's a large canvas, maybe two metres across, very dark background, almost black, and in the centre there's a figure that's — it's not quite human, it's the suggestion of a figure, like someone has tried to paint a person and the paint has remembered them imperfectly. the hands are wrong. they're too long or the fingers are in the wrong place. but the face — there's no face, there's just where the face would be. and the whole painting has this quality of something just finished leaving. I want to write into this. I don't know how yet.
